name: The Hard Problem of Consciousness
statement: Why is any of the brain's physical activity accompanied by subjective experience at all?
statementAccent: accompanied by subjective experience at all
meaning: The hard problem of consciousness is the problem of explaining why and how physical processes in the brain give rise to subjective experience, why there is something it is like to be a conscious being at all. The term was coined by the philosopher David Chalmers in a 1995 paper, Facing Up to the Problem of Consciousness, and elaborated in his 1996 book The Conscious Mind. Chalmers distinguished the hard problem from what he called the easy problems of consciousness. The easy problems are those of explaining various cognitive functions and abilities, such as the ability to discriminate and react to stimuli, the integration of information, the reportability of mental states, the focus of attention, the deliberate control of behavior, and the difference between wakefulness and sleep. These are easy, in principle, because they seem susceptible to explanation by the standard methods of cognitive science, in terms of computational or neural mechanisms. The hard problem is different: even a complete mechanistic account of all these functions seems to leave unexplained why any of this functioning is accompanied by subjective, felt experience, or phenomenal consciousness. This appears to resist functional and mechanistic explanation, and it is what Chalmers called the really hard problem, the problem of experience. It is one of the most influential framings in the philosophy of mind and the study of consciousness.
mechanism: The hard problem is defined by contrast with the easy problems of consciousness, and the contrast reveals why it is hard. The easy problems concern the objective functions and behaviors associated with consciousness: how the brain discriminates stimuli, integrates information, reports on its own states, directs attention, controls behavior, and switches between waking and sleep. Chalmers argued that these problems, though technically difficult, are easy in principle because we know what a solution would look like, namely a specification of the computational or neural mechanism that performs the function, and cognitive science is in the business of finding such mechanisms. The hard problem arises when we ask a further question: granting a complete explanation of all these functions, why is their performance accompanied by subjective experience, by there being something it is like to see red, feel pain, or taste coffee. A mechanistic account explains what the brain does, but it seems not to explain why doing it should feel like anything at all, since one can apparently imagine all the functions being carried out in the dark, without any accompanying experience. This is why the hard problem resists the methods that dissolve the easy problems. Chalmers drew on Thomas Nagel's question of what it is like to be a bat and on the explanatory gap named by Joseph Levine, and he concluded that reductive physical explanation inevitably fails on the hard problem, proposing instead a nonreductive account of consciousness.

examples.text: Explaining functions like discrimination, information integration, reportability, and attention are the easy problems, tractable by cognitive science.
The hard problem asks why all that functioning is accompanied by subjective experience, why there is something it is like at all.
Chalmers drew on Thomas Nagel's question of what it is like to be a bat to frame the subjective character of experience.

variants.name: The easy versus hard distinction
variants.text: The contrast between explaining cognitive functions, which cognitive science can address, and explaining why they are felt at all.

variants.name: Illusionism and denial
variants.text: The view of Dennett and illusionists like Frankish that the hard problem is illusory or that phenomenal consciousness is an illusion.

whyItMatters: The hard problem of consciousness is one of the most influential framings in modern philosophy of mind and the interdisciplinary study of consciousness, sharpening the central mystery of how subjective experience fits into the physical world. By distinguishing the tractable easy problems, the explanation of cognitive functions, from the hard problem of why any of that functioning is accompanied by felt experience, David Chalmers gave clear form to the intuition that consciousness poses a special explanatory challenge that ordinary scientific methods may not meet. This framing has structured decades of debate across philosophy, neuroscience, psychology, and cognitive science, organizing arguments between physicalism, which holds that consciousness is ultimately physical, and dualism and related views that deny it can be fully reduced. It connects to Thomas Nagel's question of what it is like to be a bat, to the explanatory gap, and to the knowledge argument, and it drives ongoing scientific efforts to find the neural correlates of consciousness and to ask whether experience can be explained at all. Whether one thinks the hard problem is genuine or illusory, it has become the reference point for thinking about consciousness.

working.text: explain the cognitive functions of consciousness, like discrimination and reportability, in terms of mechanisms.
observe that even a full mechanistic account seems not to explain why any of it is accompanied by subjective experience.
confront the question of why there is something it is like to undergo these processes at all.

limits: The hard problem of consciousness is a framing, not an established fact, and whether it is a genuine problem is itself hotly contested. A number of prominent philosophers deny that it is real. Daniel Dennett argues that the supposed extra fact of phenomenal experience beyond the functions is confused and that the hard problem will dissolve as the easy problems are solved. Patricia and Paul Churchland, from a neurophilosophical standpoint, treat the intuition of an unexplained residue as a philosopher's construction rather than a genuine explanandum. Illusionists such as Keith Frankish, with Dennett, hold that phenomenal consciousness is an introspective illusion, so that there are no phenomenal properties to explain, only the strong disposition to believe there are, replacing the hard problem with the problem of explaining that illusion.
misreadings: The hard problem is not the problem of explaining how the brain performs cognitive functions; those are the easy problems that cognitive science can address, and the hard problem is why any of them is felt at all. It is not universally accepted as genuine, since Dennett and illusionists argue it is confused or that phenomenal consciousness is an illusion. And it is not a claim that consciousness is definitely non-physical, but a challenge that physicalists must meet, so treating the hard problem as just the neural explanation of function, as an agreed fact, or as proving dualism, misreads an influential and contested framing.
origin: A framing coined by the philosopher David Chalmers in his 1995 paper Facing Up to the Problem of Consciousness, distinguishing the problem of why physical processes give rise to subjective experience from the easy problems of explaining cognitive function.
